items.title: Shocking Legal Win For Nigerian Woman Under Threat After Converting From Islam to Christianity
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A persecution watchdog is speaking out about a shocking case surrounding a Nigerian woman who scored a surprising legal victory after reportedly being detained and beaten for converting from Islam to Christianity.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Brad Brandon, CEO of Across Nigeria, recently returned from an extended trip to Nigeria, where he saw and experienced firsthand the horrific persecution impacing so many believers there. He joined CBN News to share that experience and to reflect on Sarah, the Nigerian woman whose court case is making international headlines.

“This is typically what happens,” he said of Sarah’s plight. “This happens, I mean … hundreds of times — thousands of times — a year in northern Nigeria. … 12 of the northern Nigerian states are controlled by Sharia law.”

Brandon said there’s a doctrine observed in many Muslim families there that a person who converts to Christianity has committed a crime – one that can sometimes be punishable by death. Sarah found herself in the crosshairs of this very dynamic.

“Your family can either kill you, or they can hire somebody to kill you, and that’s what’s going on in this case,” he said of Sarah. “So she converted to Christianity, and she felt threatened by her community and her family. She escaped that situation. Oftentimes, people will escape those situations with the help of other people.”

Sarah was in this camp as she found a Christian family to flee to after her siblings allegedly tried to force her into a marriage. The young woman stayed with this family, who helped rescue her and provide a safe haven; they were also reportedly involved in her conversion to Christianity.

As a result of their actions, the family also faces retribution.

“What they were accused of then is kidnapping,” he said. “And, again, all of these things, all of these details in this story, you could plug them into any other story. It’s the same thing that happens anywhere else.”

While a judge recently ruled in Sarah’s favor, deciding her rights were impeded when she was reportedly arrested, beaten, and mistreated for her conversion to Christianity, the family who helped her continues to face legal challenges.

items.title: Gang Members Violently Murder Christians, Torch Church
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: PRAY.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

At least 47 people and 22 others were injured Sunday night into Monday morning when gang members attacked a church providing shelter to displaced peoples right outside Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince.

The mayor of Kenscoff, Massillon Jean, said the deadly assault began around 10:30 p.m. and described it as a “night of terror.”

Jean blamed the Viv Ansanm gang coalition, one of the largest groups of violent gang members in Haiti.

According to an official statement, the Haitian government sent reinforcements to help local area police.

“Let there be no mistake: this time of mourning is also a challenge,” said the press release. “And to this challenge, the government responds with the force of law and the legitimate exercise of state force.”

It continued, “All security forces have been placed on maximum alert. Reinforcements are being deployed. The orders are clear: protect, secure, intervene. Government authority will be restored — firmly and without delay — throughout the entire territory of Kenscoff.”

The government added “no armed group will thrive in Haiti” and “[c]riminals will find no truce, no refuge, and no impunity.”

Haitian Bishop Joseph Gontrand Décoste of Jérémie told Aid to the Church in Need (ACN) that churches and Christians as a whole are increasingly the targets of gang violence because believers remain the last stalwart resistance against wrongdoing.

“We are the last remaining bulkhead — moral, ethical, spiritual, and prophetic,” he said. “That is why they want to eliminate us.”

For context, about 40 Catholic parishes have shut down in Port-au-Prince as Christians have faced increasingly deadly violence. In the first seven months of 2026, two priests were abducted and a seminarian was murdered. Last spring, two nuns from the Little Sisters of Saint Thérèse were killed and, in 2024, nine religious sisters, five brothers, and four priests were kidnapped.

ACN has reported gangs control somewhere between 70% and 90% of the capital city of Port-au-Prince.

items.title: Christ in Me
items.author: Jennifer Benson Schuldt
items.summary: Renaissance artist Albrecht Dürer became famous for his talent at age twenty. The art critics of his day called him “the greatest mind that ever expressed itself in line.” As his fame spread, influential people tried to hire him with promises of luxury and ease. Even other acclaimed
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Renaissance artist Albrecht Dürer became famous for his talent at age twenty. The art critics of his day called him “the greatest mind that ever expressed itself in line.” As his fame spread, influential people tried to hire him with promises of luxury and ease. Even other acclaimed artists such as Giovanni Bellini and Raphael revered his work.

In what experts consider to be his best self-portrait, Dürer mingled his physical characteristics with what he thought Jesus might have looked like. He painted himself with long wavy hair, a beard, and eyes that seemed to convey a sense of divine purpose. Many assumed this piece was a prideful statement about the artist’s opinion of himself. Others who were familiar with his virtuous character believed the painting wasn’t blasphemous or big-headed but aspirational. They believed Dürer wanted to live a life that would allow people to see Jesus in him.

If we truly know Christ, this is our desire as well. Believing in Him and accepting His death and resurrection as the basis for our relationship with God means we should now live for Jesus—not for ourselves (Galatians 2:19). We live for Him and He lives in us and works through us. The apostle Paul said this about his spiritual transformation: “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (v. 20). May the glory of Christ shine through our lives today so that the world sees Him in us.

items.title: God’s Rich Provision
items.author: Patricia Raybon
items.summary: After Hurricane Helene’s floodwaters nearly destroyed his small North Carolina town in 2024, a pastor noticed an inspiring pattern. As he struggled to answer the persistent question, “What do you need?” donations kept showing up exactly when he needed them. Phone chargers? Out of t
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

After Hurricane Helene’s floodwaters nearly destroyed his small North Carolina town in 2024, a pastor noticed an inspiring pattern. As he struggled to answer the persistent question, “What do you need?” donations kept showing up exactly when he needed them. Phone chargers? Out of the blue, a man drove up with a generator, creating a charging station at the church. Drinking water? Suddenly, pallets of water bottles arrived.

Coincidence? The Bible points us to God, not mere happenstance. “My God will meet all your needs according to the riches of His glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19). The promise might seem empty to a town nearly demolished by a thirty-foot wall of raging water. But Paul, who was in prison when he offered this encouragement, was no stranger to hardship.

Paul was writing to the church in Philippi to thank them for badly needed financial gifts. Except for them, he’d been neglected (v. 15). But God used them to meet his needs. So, His words shined a bright light on God who provided the “riches of His glory” found in Christ Jesus our Savior, in whom we have “every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3). Joy, peace, truth, salvation are among the needs He richly provides. In kindness as well, He’ll provide a drink of water too, if that’s what we need. What a loving, generous God.

items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: Russell Wilson’s last season ended with him watching. He signed a one-year deal with the Giants expecting to start, was benched three games in for a rookie, Jaxson Dart, and retired on June 3 after 14 seasons. He’s 37, a Super Bowl champion and a 10-time Pro Bowler, and that was the fini
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Russell Wilson’s last season ended with him watching. He signed a one-year deal with the Giants expecting to start, was benched three games in for a rookie, Jaxson Dart, and retired on June 3 after 14 seasons. He’s 37, a Super Bowl champion and a 10-time Pro Bowler, and that was the finish.

On Friday he was in Rio de Janeiro, at the foot of Christ the Redeemer, and he posted the photos with four words: “Christ is more than enough!”

Underneath them he put Psalm 46:1 — “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.”

Which is to say the verse he chose is the one about God being a refuge in trouble, and the caption he chose is about what’s left when the thing you were known for is over.

Wilson has been public about his faith for his entire career, so none of this is a departure. What’s different is the timing.

The post has just under 50,000 likes. This is the first fall since 2012 that Wilson isn’t playing football.

items.title: ‘Strange Vocations’: A New and Welcomed Conversation About Priestly Eligibility
items.author: Mark Bradford
items.summary:
Mark Bradford

It may seem strange to recommend that autistic men be accepted into seminaries to become priests. But it would be stranger to resist investigating the possibility.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Mark Bradford

In 1990, Pope St. John Paul II recognized the crisis in priestly vocations and the need for improved formation of men capable of responding to cultural challenges brought on “by the deep and rapid transformations in the societies and culture of our age.” To address the issue, he convened a synod of bishops to address the “Formation of Priests in the Circumstances of the Present Day,” and in 1992, he presented a post-synodal apostolic exhortation titled Pastores Dabo Vobis, or “I Will Give You Shepherds.” In it he introduced a new area to be addressed in seminary formation he called “human formation.” The goal was to develop priests who were affectively mature and better prepared to serve their flocks as a cultural and spiritual bridge to an encounter with Christ rather than an obstacle burdened by unresolved cultural baggage. 

This year, Notre Dame’s McGrath Center for Church Life published a set of twelve proposals they suggest for assessing the suitability of men for the priesthood. Their recommendations were drawn from a study they had commissioned in 2024 from the Center for Applied Research in the Apostolate (CARA) at Georgetown University on how dioceses and seminaries assess seminarians’ suitability for ordination. The McGrath Center fortified the CARA study through conversations with seminary rectors, psychologists, and others involved in forming men to assume spiritual leadership in the Church through Holy Orders. The CARA study and those conversations are distilled into these twelve proposals. 

The McGrath Center divides the twelve proposals into three sections. The recommendations lean heavily into contemporary issues that impact their suitability to serve as priests, including their psychological health (Section One) and chastity (Section Three). What especially caught my eye, however, was Section Two, which encourages exploring the possibility of admitting men into formation who may be autistic, have ADHD, OCD, or other “significant formative deficits,” as the document calls them. This is a very new and welcome addition to the conversation on who is eligible to study and be formed as priests to offer themselves in a life of service to Christ and his Church. 

The topic of admitting persons with disabilities to Holy Orders challenges the current paradigm of who the ideal candidate for the priesthood might be. As I read this report, I was reminded of a book review I published in Evangelization and Culture Online in October 2024. The book was written by Dr. Amy Richards and called Disability in Classical Education. In it, she presented this curious phrase, “strange vocations” to suggest the unique place that persons with disabilities might occupy in schools. I believe that term, when properly understood, may be both clarifying and challenging to the Church as it considers what roles persons with disabilities might successfully fill in the Church of the future.

Dr. Richards drew her phrase “strange vocations” from St. Augustine (miris vocationibus in Latin and found in Book 1, chapter 22, section 32 of this treatise) and interprets it in the context of how he explains disability in City of God (Book 16, chapter 8). She then adds what the Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches, that it is “through the exchange with others, [and] mutual service and dialogue with his brethren, [that] man develops his potential; [and] thus responds to his vocation” (No. 1879). St. Augustine provides the logic of why a person with a disability might be a hidden gift to the Church rather than a problem to solve. He refuses to see what he termed “monstrous births”—persons with physical or intellectual “defects”—as a divine failure and instead sees them contributing to the beauty of the whole, a beauty that perhaps only God can perceive. This “strangeness” is woven into the fabric of life by our divine Creator to challenge our “cult of normalcy” and cause us to look deeper into acknowledging the extent to which we are all vulnerable. 

This view of disability—as revelatory of our mutual vulnerability—is echoed by the International Theological Commission’s recent document, Quo Vadis Humanitas, which encourages theological reflection on disability to come to terms with two universals in all human experience: vulnerability and dependence (see my reflections on paragraph 118 of this document here). 

Dr. Michael Waddell, the Edna and George McMahon Aquinas Chair in Philosophy at Saint Mary’s College and founder of their Autism Studies program, is indirectly helpful in bringing these voices together on the topic of disability and vocation in the Church. Dr. Waddell’s understanding of autistic identity is that it is uniquely relational as is seen in the way that autistic persons bond with one another to form profoundly meaningful relationships. Their self-understanding, or identity, is formed in community with other autistic persons. I encourage you to listen to Dr. Waddell’s excellent lecture on this topic, while keeping in mind the Catechism’s comments that vocational discernment is found in exchange with others. 

The increased prevalence of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has been widely covered over the last few years in the media, and its cause is hotly contested. The CDC’s latest statistic (2022) for the incidence of autism in the US is about 1 in 31 (or 3.2 percent) of children who are eight years old. In the mid-1990s, the reported incidence was only about 1 in 500, but older statistics were drawn from different diagnostic criteria and are only minimally helpful in understanding the rate of increase. However, it is reasonable to state that, at least under the current diagnostic criteria, the incidence of autism is in fact increasing in the US and therefore in the Church as well. Added to the pediatric numbers, adult diagnosis of ASD increased in the decade from 2011 to 2022 by 175 percent. The same source reports that autism in young adults between 26 and 34 increased during the same period by 450 percent! 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

We can be certain that the population statistics represent the number of Catholics with autism, and we can assume that the number will continue to grow, creating a substantial need in the Church for priests who are comfortable and capable of ministering to a population that self-identifies through their relationships with one another. And what better ministers could there be to this population, and to all Catholics, than autistic men who through proper formation and care are perfectly capable of carrying out priestly ministry in the Church. 

The McGrath Center report acknowledges the challenges autism presents, such as reduced empathy, difficulty with social cues, emotional rigidity, and others; but they continue to report that “It is important to acknowledge that these traits can appear in any given candidate, and not just those on the ASD spectrum” (Recommendation 7). Just like all candidates for the priesthood, these men would need to be successful in their formation and to be able to respond well to “specialized mentoring and psychotherapy to help them develop the relational capacities necessary for ministry.” Presumably, those who apply would understand the challenges they would face as autistics and be willing to assume the possible burden of masking some behaviors in order to serve in a pastoral role. Of course, they would also need to otherwise prove themselves suitable for Holy Orders. The McGrath Center has formed a task force to investigate the subject more fully. 

So, it may seem strange to see a recommendation that autistic men be accepted into seminaries to become priests. But it would be stranger to resist investigating the possibility, leaving willing men who wish to serve on the sidelines. And yes, that growing number of autistic Catholics would be most grateful too.

items.title: WOF 543 | Christian Charity vs. “Suicidal Empathy”
items.author: Dr. Matthew Petrusek
items.summary:
Dr. Matthew Petrusek

What role should the biblical conception of love play in defining what it means to show true compassion and care for those in need?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Welcome back to the Word on Fire Show. I’m Matthew Petrusek, senior director of the Word on Fire Institute and the host of the Word on Fire Show. Thank you for joining us. The evolutionary behavioral scientist and public intellectual Gad Saad recently published an influential book entitled Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind. In it, Saad argues that much of the West has, unfortunately, come to embrace a perversely deficient understanding of empathy, twisting the natural and otherwise noble human capacity to feel and respond to other peoples’ sufferings into a moral license to upend the moral, economic, and political order. According to the dictates of suicidal empathy, for example, society should prioritize criminals over victims, illegal immigrants over citizens, lawbreakers over law abiders, racial identity over competence, adult sexual expression over childhood innocence, and trans women––that is, men pretending to be women––over real women. Suicidal empathy’s endgame, Saad warns, is nothing less than societal ruin and the eventual totalitarian eclipse of the individual. How, from a Catholic perspective, should we assess these claims? Is Saad’s characterization of suicidal empathy and its dangers accurate? If so, how should we, as Christians, constructively respond? What role, in particular, should the biblical conception of love play in defining what it means to show true compassion and care for those in need? Here to discuss Saad’s book and to explain how authentic Christian charity is—and is not—related to empathy, is Bishop Robert Barron.
